scenes.name: one turn, thirty milliseconds
scenes.visual: Dark canvas, one continuous shot. It opens on the generate-loop panel rebuilt as it stood at the end of ch01_s05 b2, not as that scene ended: a large rounded panel (x 200-1720, y 300-800) titled 'the generate loop'. Inside, left to right: a blue box 'text so far' holding ch01's nine pills in two rows, 'the quick brown fox jumps' over 'over the lazy dog'; an arrow; a coral box 'run the whole model' with the small 40-tile weight grid inside it (coral means a weight being read); an arrow; a blue box 'one new token'. A return arrow runs from 'one new token' down and back along the panel's bottom edge to 'text so far', labelled 'append, go round again'. No 'model runs' counter, no '300', no equation and no takeaway. New here: a stopwatch icon at (1600, 215), above the panel's top right, showing '?'. From b2 the panel scales to 55% and parks in the top band (centre 960, 250), still turning slowly at 40% opacity; the centre band (y 560) becomes a one-second ruler and the bottom band (y 700-880) a compact copy of ch00's chat window. In b3 the chat window fades and two labels take the bottom band. In b4 everything fades back except the stopwatch reading, and ch00's spec-sheet card returns. Colour: tokens blue, the expensive model step coral, the spec sheet's compute line amber and memory line coral, text white and grey. The idea: one turn is one token is about 30 ms; laid end to end that is a stream at least as fast as reading, which is the target; and the number can be derived.

beats.say: One turn of the generate loop, draw included, takes about thirty milliseconds, three hundredths of a second.
beats.show: The panel is on screen from the first frame; the stopwatch with its '?' fades in above its top right. On 'One turn', copies of the nine pills flow into the coral box and its tiles light top to bottom; the '?' becomes '0 ms' and the stopwatch starts. On 'the generate loop', the panel's title glows once. On 'draw included', as the last tiles light, the small spinner from ch01's sampling scene flickers once at the left edge of 'one new token'. On 'thirty milliseconds', a new blue pill '.' pops into 'one new token' and the stopwatch stops at '30 ms'; a small grey tag under it reads 'slowed down', since the turn took about two seconds of screen time. On 'three hundredths', a grey line writes under the reading: '= 0.03 s'.

beats.say: That is about thirty-three tokens a second, words arriving at least as fast as you read.
beats.show: The '.' pill rides the return arrow and appends to the row. The panel scales to 55% and slides into the top band at 40% opacity, still turning slowly; the stopwatch keeps reading '30 ms'. In the centre band a ruler draws from x 260 to x 1660, '0' to '1 s', ticks every 0.1 s, so 1,400 px is one second. Blue pills drop onto it one every 42 px, which is every 30 ms, slowed 4× so the second fills in about four seconds; grey tag under the ruler's left end: 'slowed 4×'. On 'thirty-three tokens', a counter above the ruler's right end (1560, 480) starts, and it reaches 33 as the last pill lands, label 'tokens in 1 s'. In the bottom band ch00's chat window returns with 'Why is the sky blue?', its answer streaming on the same 4× clock as the ruler, each token landing as a blue pill and relaxing into text. On 'as fast as you read', the newest words glow softly as they land. Add no eye icon or reading-pace marker: real reading is far slower than this stream, and a marker would make 33 look far above the slowest acceptable pace.

beats.say: That is the target, and not an arbitrary one: roughly the slowest pace that still reads smoothly.
beats.show: The 'slowed 4×' tag fades and the chat window fades out, its job done. On 'the target', a white check-circle icon and the label 'the target' land just right of the counter, left edge at (1640, 480). On 'not an arbitrary one', a grey label writes in the bottom band, centred at (960, 760): 'not arbitrary'. On 'roughly the slowest pace', a white label lands beneath it, centred at (960, 830): 'rule of thumb: slowest that still reads smoothly'. The ruler keeps its 30 ms beat throughout; the counter's '33' glows once on 'smoothly'.

beats.say: Soon you will derive it from the model's size and a chip's specification sheet.
beats.show: The panel, ruler, counter, check-circle and labels fade to 20%. The stopwatch's '30 ms' lifts off, enlarges and settles centre top (960, 290) as a white stamp '≈ 30 ms per token', with a small grey line under it: 'the number this film is about'. On 'derive it', ch00's spec-sheet card slides up beneath it (x 700-1220, y 400-800): header 'chip spec sheet' and six grey placeholder lines. On 'the model's size', the coral 'run the whole model' box in the faded panel brightens briefly, then dims back. On 'specification sheet', two of the lines brighten and resolve exactly as in ch00: amber 'operations per second: ?' and coral 'bytes per second: ?'. No chip-and-model riffle here; ch00 already played it. Hold.

scenes.name: one file, three homes
scenes.visual: One continuous shot: three capacity bars on one true scale, then the read speeds of the two that hold the whole file. Top band: the equation (centred, y 165) and, under it, the model as a solid coral block (x 200-1200, y 235-285). Three rows, all starting at x 200, each with an icon and a two-part title above its bar: disk (title y 350, bar y 375-425), memory beside the chip (title y 545, bar y 570-620), the chip itself (title y 740, bar y 765-815). Scale: 1,000 px = 140 GB. The memory bar is exactly 1,000 px: a memory sized to fit the model, schematic rather than a particular chip (real chips' capacities come in the three-chip scene). The disk bar runs off the right edge of the frame: truncated, not shrunk, so the scale still holds. The chip bar at this scale is 0.87 px, drawn as a 1 px hairline. Right zone (x 1260-1820) holds the magnifier and the two stopwatches. Colour: bars are blue outlines (containers), the model's bytes coral, the chip's working areas amber outlines, text white and grey. The takeaway band (y 952) is used in b5. The idea: one file, three homes of wildly different size and speed; once the model is running the disk drops out, and the story is the memory beside the chip.

beats.say: File sizes are counted in bytes, and each weight takes two. So seventy billion weights make a hundred and forty billion bytes, a hundred and forty gigabytes.
beats.show: A file icon at (250, 165) opens into a small grid of coral weight tiles. On 'counted in bytes', a grey caption writes right of the grid, left-anchored at (420, 140): 'file sizes: counted in bytes'. On 'each weight takes two', one tile enlarges in place, and the tag '2 bytes' lands under the caption at (420, 200), with a small grey tag after it on the same line: 'why two: later'. On 'seventy billion', the caption and both tags fade, and the equation builds term by term, centred at y 165: '70,000,000,000 weights', then '× 2 bytes', then '= 140,000,000,000 bytes' on 'a hundred and forty billion bytes', which morphs into '= 140 GB' on 'gigabytes'; a grey note writes under its right end: '1 GB = 1 billion bytes'. The tile grid compresses into the solid coral block (x 200-1200, y 235-285) labelled '140 GB'.

beats.say: It lives in three places. A disk stores it. The memory beside the chip holds it while the model runs. The chip itself, which does the arithmetic, holds almost nothing.
beats.show: The equation and its grey note fade out, leaving the coral block and its '140 GB' label in the top band. On 'A disk', a hard-drive icon and the title 'A disk · keeps it between uses' appear and the disk bar draws from x 200 rightward and off the frame edge; a copy of the coral block at 60% opacity slides into its left end; grey tag at the frame's right edge, above the bar: 'far more →'. On 'the memory beside the chip', a memory-module icon and the title 'Memory beside the chip · in use' appear and its bar draws to exactly 1,000 px; on 'while the model runs', the top coral block drops into it and fills it edge to edge, and a grey tag writes just above the bar's right end, right-aligned at (1200, 548): 'sized to fit the model'. On 'The chip itself', a cpu icon and the title 'The chip itself · does the arithmetic' appear; on 'almost nothing', its bar draws as a 1 px hairline at x 200, with a grey tag beside it: 'to scale: under 1 px'.

beats.say: A few hundred thousand bytes in each small working area, a tenth of a gigabyte in all.
beats.show: The disk tag, the 'sized to fit the model' tag and the chip's 'to scale' tag dim to 30%. A magnifier circle, radius 120, swings from the hairline to (1500, 800), joined to it by a thin line, and enlarges it: inside, a grid of many small amber-outlined squares, the chip's working areas. On 'each small working area', one square highlights and a label lands left of the circle, right-aligned at x 1360, y 840: 'each: a few hundred thousand bytes'. On 'a tenth of a gigabyte', a second label lands above it at y 780: '≈ 0.1 GB in all · ≈ 1/1,000 of the model'.

beats.say: Reading it all off a fast disk takes about twenty seconds. From the memory beside the chip, tens of milliseconds.
beats.show: The magnifier and its labels dim to 30%; the three titles dim to 60%. Both reads run on one clock, time-compressed 10×; grey tag at (1500, 245): '10× time-compressed'. On 'off a fast disk', coral particles trickle out of the disk's block along a thin path down the left margin (x 170) into the chip's hairline: the what-if of the chip reading the disk directly. A grey tag writes at the path's top, left-anchored at (215, 455) just under the disk bar: 'if read straight from disk'. Meanwhile a stopwatch above the disk bar at (1500, 300) counts up for two seconds of screen time to '≈ 20 s'; grey note right-aligned beside it at x 1450: 'fast drive ≈ 7 GB/s · varies'. On 'tens of milliseconds', the memory block fires one dense burst along its own short path into the hairline, over within a single frame (about 4 ms on the same 10× clock); its stopwatch at (1500, 595), right of the memory bar, snaps to 'tens of ms'. A white bracket joins the two stopwatches on their right (x 1790, y 300-595), with the label '≈ 500× faster' at (1620, 490), between the disk and memory rows.

beats.say: So the model is loaded once, at start-up, and stays put. The disk plays no part in making tokens. This film lives in the memory beside the chip.
beats.show: Stopwatches, bracket, notes and the 10× tag dim to 30%; the disk-to-chip particle path and its 'if read straight from disk' tag fade out, since the real route is drawn next. On 'loaded once', a coral arrow draws from the disk's block down to the memory bar, labelled 'load once, at start-up', and the memory block flashes once. On 'stays put', a grey label writes under the memory bar at (200, 655): 'stays while the service runs'. On 'plays no part', the whole disk row fades to 20% and its 'far more →' tag swaps to 'start-up only, never per token'. On 'This film lives', the memory bar glows and the takeaway lands: 'memory beside the chip: this film's home'.

scenes.name: paid once, spread thin
scenes.visual: One continuous shot along a single timeline: the life of the service, start-up at the left. The timeline runs across the centre (x 200-1720, y 520). At its left, a coral block 'load: many seconds' (schematic, 180 px wide at first); right of it an arrow, then a long blue band 'serve: a token every 30 ms' that fills with tiny blue tick marks, one per token. Top band: a token counter (centre, y 300) with a grey worked line under it (y 360). Lower third: a worked line (y 690) over a pair of bars drawn to one scale (y 770 and 830, both starting at x 460). Teal labels land above the timeline (y 440) in the last beat. The idea: a one-off cost shrinks to nothing when shared over millions of tokens; then a hint of a cost that every token pays again.

beats.say: Picture the model's working life: a load of many seconds, then a token every thirty milliseconds, for hours.
beats.show: On 'a load', the coral block 'load: many seconds' draws at the far left. On 'a token every thirty milliseconds', an arrow draws on and the blue band 'serve: a token every 30 ms' unrolls rightward to x 1720, filling with tiny ticks at a steady rhythm. On 'for hours', a grey label appears at the right end: 'hours →'.

beats.say: The load is real, but paid once. Shared among a day's millions of tokens, it is about seven millionths of a second each.
beats.show: On 'paid once', a small white tag '× 1' pins to the load block. On 'a day's', the timeline rescales to a full day: the right label becomes '24 hours', the ticks merge into a dense blue band, and the load block shrinks to its true width, a 0.35 px sliver, marked by a grey pointer 'load'. The top-band counter runs 0 to 2,880,000, label 'tokens', with the grey line under it 'one conversation, all day: 86,400 s ÷ 0.03 s'. On 'seven millionths', the lower third writes 'load share = 20 s ÷ 2,880,000 ≈ 7 millionths of a second'; beneath it, a blue bar 1,000 px long labelled '30 ms: the token itself' and, at the same left edge, a coral dot with a pointer 'load share', a quarter of a pixel at this scale; grey tag '≈ 0.02%'.

beats.say: A fixed cost stops mattering once spread over enough work. That is amortising, and it comes back often. Next comes a cost that, one token at a time, refuses to spread.
beats.show: The counter and the lower third dim to 30%. On 'a fixed cost', a teal label lands above the timeline: 'fixed cost ÷ lots of work → tiny'; on 'amortising', the word 'amortising' writes under it in teal; on 'comes back often', a small grey tag settles just right of the word: 'first of many'. On 'Next comes a cost', the teal labels and the tag dim and the camera pushes in on the timeline's right end. On 'one token at a time', three consecutive ticks grow into blue token pills, one after another, each topped by its own coral block as wide as the load block was before it shrank (180 px), labelled '140 GB': the same bytes the load moved, now apparently paid again by every token. On 'refuses to spread', a '?' settles above the row with the label 'paid again, every token?'.

scenes.name: every token reads every weight
scenes.visual: One continuous shot. Centre-left: a GPU package seen from above (x 260-1240, y 330-830): the compute die in the middle, amber outline, label 'the chip · does the arithmetic'; two HBM stacks either side, blue containers full of coral weight tiles, label 'memory beside the chip · 140 GB'; joined to the die by a wide bus of parallel lines. Top band (y 165): the rule builds as an equation. Right column (x 1360-1820): first two counters, later the spec-sheet card from the opening scene. A label line under the package at y 880. The idea: the chip cannot keep the weights, so for one conversation every token drags all 140 GB across the bus, and the rule falls straight out of the picture.

beats.say: Here is that cost. Each token needs all seventy billion weights, which the chip cannot keep. So for one conversation, every token streams all hundred and forty gigabytes in from memory.
beats.show: The package fades in. On 'all seventy billion weights', the stacks fill with coral tiles. On 'cannot keep', a tiny region inside the die highlights with a grey tag '≈ 0.1 GB fits here'. On 'one conversation', a user icon with one blue pill appears just right of the die. Three runs follow, each keyed to its own words. On 'every token streams', run 1 (about 1.2 s): coral particles flow along the bus in slices; as each slice arrives the die flashes amber for an instant and the slice fades; the counter 'bytes moved, this token' (1590, 400) runs 0 to 140 GB, a blue token pill pops out of the die, and 'tokens' (1590, 500) reads 1. On 'hundred and forty gigabytes', run 2 (about 0.8 s): the counter resets and runs 0 to 140 GB again, a second pill pops out, 'tokens' reads 2. On 'from memory', run 3 (about 0.6 s), the same, and 'tokens' reads 3 as the beat ends. As the beat ends, a label writes under the package: 'one conversation: all 140 GB, every token'; small grey tag at its right end: 'shared reads, many users: later'.

beats.say: Time per token is the bytes to read, divided by the bytes the memory delivers each second, its bandwidth. Hence the name, high bandwidth memory, H B M.
beats.show: The counters and the user icon fade out; the bus keeps flowing at a steady rate. The equation builds term by term on the spoken words: 'time per token' (white), '=', 'bytes to read' (coral), '÷' on 'divided by', 'bytes per second' (coral) on 'each second'. On 'bandwidth', a bracket draws under 'bytes per second' labelled 'bandwidth'. On 'high bandwidth memory', the stack label becomes 'HBM · high bandwidth memory'. The die label and the line under the package dim to 40%.

beats.say: Bandwidth is one of those two specification numbers. The other, how fast the chip calculates, does not even appear.
beats.show: The line under the package fades and, as the beat begins, the spec-sheet card from the opening scene slides into the right column (x 1380-1800, y 380-720) with its two lines, amber 'operations per second: ?' and coral 'bytes per second: ?'. On 'Bandwidth is one', the coral line brightens and a thin coral connector draws from it up to the equation's 'bytes per second'. On 'the other', the amber line pulses; on 'does not even appear', a white highlight sweeps the equation left to right and finds no amber term, and the amber line dims to 40% with a grey tag 'not in the rule'; at the same moment a small amber tag settles beside the die, saying why: 'arithmetic ≈ 0.1 ms · overlaps the reading (later)'.

scenes.name: three chips, one division
scenes.visual: One continuous shot: one division done for three chips. Top band (y 165): 'time per token = 140 GB ÷ bandwidth', with 140 GB and bandwidth in coral. Directly below (y 245), a single centred worked-line band that holds one line at a time and is replaced row by row. A three-row table below it, rows centred at y 390, 530 and 670. Left column (x 120-500): chip cards, each a chip icon with name and bandwidth: 'H100 · 3.35 TB/s', 'H200 · 4.8 TB/s', 'B200 · 8 TB/s', with room for a small grey capacity tag under the name. Middle: coral bars from a common baseline at x 540, drawn to scale at 20 px per millisecond: 836, 583 and 350 px, ending at x 1376, 1123 and 890. Each value sits left-anchored 16 px past its bar's end, except the H200's '29.2 ms': that bar stops only 17 px short of the 30 ms line, so its value sits just past the line, left-anchored at x 1160, and nothing touches the line. A dashed vertical line at 30 ms (x 1140, y 340-720), labelled '30 ms' at its foot; the space just above its top, around (1140, 312), is kept free for the b2 stamp. Grey tag under the table at (540, 760): 'bars to scale'. Right column (x 1620-1800): 'tokens / s', filled in the last two beats, with about 42 px free under each cell for a small badge. The H100 value '41.8 ms' ends near x 1530, so nothing docks beside the cells. Takeaway band (y 952) used in b5. The idea: thirty milliseconds is a division, and a figure that seems to clash with it is the same division on a different chip.

beats.say: The memory on Nvidia's H one hundred delivers three point three five terabytes a second, a terabyte being a thousand gigabytes. So each token takes forty-one point eight milliseconds.
beats.show: On 'Nvidia's H one hundred', the three cards slide in, H100 bright and the other two at 50%. On 'a terabyte being a thousand gigabytes', the worked-line band writes '3.35 TB/s = 3,350 GB/s', with a small grey '1 TB = 1,000 GB' beneath. On 'forty-one point eight', the band swaps to '140 GB ÷ 3,350 GB/s = 0.0418 s' and the H100 bar grows to 836 px with '41.8 ms' just past its end. As the beat ends, a grey tag settles under the H100 name in two short lines: 'holds 80 GB: model won't fit' and 'a what-if'.

beats.say: The H two hundred takes twenty-nine point two. There are your thirty milliseconds, right on target. The B two hundred, seventeen point five.
beats.show: On 'H two hundred', its card brightens; the band swaps to '140 GB ÷ 4,800 GB/s = 0.0292 s' and the bar grows to 583 px, with '29.2 ms' placed just past the dashed line at x 1160. On 'thirty milliseconds', the row glows white and a stamp '≈ 30 ms' lands on top of the dashed line, centred at (1140, 312), above the table rather than on the row; on 'right on target', the white check-circle from the opening scene pops just right of the stamp at (1225, 312). A grey tag settles under the H200 name: 'holds 141 GB: a tight squeeze'. On 'B two hundred', its card brightens; the band swaps to '140 GB ÷ 8,000 GB/s = 0.0175 s' and the bar grows to 350 px, '17.5 ms' just past its end.

beats.say: Not a guess, not a benchmark: a division, the best the chip can do, and it moves with model size and memory speed.
beats.show: The worked line clears and the capacity tags dim to 30%. In the band, one phrase at a time, each replacing the last: 'not a guess', 'not a benchmark', then 'a division: the best case'. On 'model size', the '140 GB' in the equation pulses and briefly reads '70 GB' while all three bars shrink to half (418, 292, 175 px), hold, and spring back as '140 GB' returns. On 'memory speed', the 'bandwidth' term pulses and the three bandwidth labels on the cards pulse top to bottom.

beats.say: Later you will meet about twenty-four tokens a second, not thirty-three. A clash? One second divided by forty-one point eight milliseconds is twenty-three point nine, the H one hundred row.
beats.show: The band clears. On 'twenty-four tokens a second', a blue quote card lands in the band's right half: '≈ 24 tokens/s · later'; on 'not thirty-three', a second lands in its left half: '30 ms → 33 tokens/s'. On 'A clash?', a '≠' between them flickers. On 'one second divided by', the right column gets its header 'tokens / s' with a grey '= 1 s ÷ time' under it, and the H100 cell fills '23.9' on 'twenty-three point nine'. On 'the H one hundred row', the right quote card shrinks into a small badge '≈ 24 · later' and tucks under the H100 cell, centred at (1710, 432).

beats.say: Same division, different chip. Running down clashes like that is a habit worth having.
beats.show: On 'Same division', the H200 cell fills '34.3' and the B200 cell '57.1'; the left quote card shrinks into a small badge '33 · rounded from 30 ms' and tucks under the H200 cell, centred at (1710, 572), so '33' sits just below '34.3'. The '≠' left in the band morphs into '=' and fades. On 'a habit', the takeaway lands: 'same division, different chips'.

scenes.name: everything between those two boxes
scenes.visual: One continuous shot, calm and spacious. Two large rounded blue boxes on one line, centred at y 520: left (x 180-760) 'A trained checkpoint' with sub-label 'weights on disk' and, inside it, a small drive icon holding the coral 140 GB block; right (x 1160-1740) 'A service that responds' with sub-label 'a token every 30 ms', a chat bubble inside streaming words at a true 30 ms beat, and a user icon just outside its right edge (x 1790). The gap between the boxes (x 760-1160) stays unfilled, crossed only by the b2 arrow, until the last word, when the white word 'inference' fills it. The idea: the whole subject of the film sits in the gap between a file and a responsive service.

beats.say: On the left, a trained checkpoint, the saved weights. On the right, a service that responds, a token every thirty milliseconds.
beats.show: The camera eases out from a close view of the empty centre to the full wide frame as the beat begins. On 'a trained checkpoint', the left box draws on, with its sub-label 'weights on disk' and the drive icon holding the coral block. On 'a service that responds', the right box draws on with 'a token every 30 ms'; its chat bubble starts streaming and the user icon fades in.

beats.say: Training made the checkpoint. Turning it into something a person can talk to, at a price that works, is its own discipline.
beats.show: On 'Training made the checkpoint', a faded grey tag 'training: done' appears above the left box. On 'Turning it into', a white arrow draws from the left box to the right box across the gap. On 'talk to', the user icon pulses; on 'a price that works', a small price-tag icon settles on the arrow.

beats.say: Why does the reading, not the arithmetic, hold the gap between them at thirty milliseconds, not far less? That is the rest of this film. Everything between those two boxes is inference.
beats.show: On 'the reading', coral particles start flowing along the arrow. On 'not the arithmetic', a faint amber ghost label '0.1 ms?' flickers beside the right box's '30 ms' and fades. On 'the gap between them', a thin grey bracket draws under the arrow across the gap (x 760-1160, y 640). On 'thirty milliseconds', '30 ms' glows. On 'the rest of this film', the bracket fades. On 'inference', a soft white band fills the gap under the arrow and the word 'inference' writes on inside it, large. Hold for two seconds.

checks.claim: 70 billion weights × 2 bytes = 140,000,000,000 bytes = 140 GB
30 ms = 0.03 s, three hundredths of a second
one second of output at 30 ms per token ≈ 33 tokens

'at least as fast as you read': at a common estimate of 250 words a minute and ~1.5 tokens per word (ch01), reading is ≈ 6 tokens/s, ≈ 160 ms per token; 33 tokens/s is ≈ 5× that, so the claim holds with room to spare. Because real reading is that much slower, s01 shows no eye icon or reading-pace marker, which would make 33 look far above 'the slowest pace that still reads smoothly' (a rule of thumb, kept on screen as one; fig 11's 'responsive to a reader', worded as reading pace so 'responsive' stays with the first-token pause, as in ch17 and fig 143). Estimate, not from the atlas
s01 ruler: 1,400 px per second puts one pill every 42 px (30 ms); 33 pills in the second
disk: 140 GB at ≈ 7 GB/s (a fast NVMe drive; illustrative) ≈ 20 s, matching atlas fig 106's 'about 20,000 ms'

CORRECTION (reviewer): disk vs memory beside the chip = 20 s ÷ 41.8 ms ≈ 479× on an H100, shown as '≈ 500× faster' to match fig 106 and ch09 ('roughly five hundred times'); it rises to ≈ 686× (H200) and ≈ 1,143× (B200). The earlier draft's '500–1,000×' understated the top end
s02.b4 runs both reads on one 10×-compressed clock: disk 20 s → 2 s of screen time; H100 memory 41.8 ms → 4.2 ms, a single frame

CORRECTION to fig 12 'the chip holds a few hundred kilobytes': true per working area (an H100 SM has a 256 KB register file + 256 KB L1/shared), but the whole H100 holds 132 × 512 KB + 50 MB L2 ≈ 0.12 GB on chip. Film says both: 'a few hundred thousand bytes in each small working area, a tenth of a gigabyte in all' (same as ch09 and ch12)
140 GB is ≈ 1,150× the on-chip storage, so the chip holds '≈ 1/1,000 of the model'

CORRECTION to fig 12 'bars roughly to scale' (atlas draws the chip bar 60 px against the memory bar's 380 px): at true scale against a 1,000 px memory bar the chip bar is 0.87 px, so the film draws a 1 px hairline under a magnifier; the disk bar is truncated at the frame edge rather than shrunk. The memory bar is exactly 1,000 px = 140 GB, tagged 'sized to fit the model' (fig 12's 'the memory holds exactly the model'): a schematic memory, not a specific chip; s05 gives real capacities (H100 80 GB, H200 141 GB)
one conversation running all day at 30 ms per token ≈ 2,880,000 tokens ('a day's millions of tokens')
a 20 s load spread over 2.88 million tokens ≈ 0.0000069 s, 'about seven millionths of a second' per token
that load share is ≈ 0.02% of a 30 ms token

s03 bars: load share against a 1,000 px bar for 30 ms ≈ a quarter of a pixel; the 20 s load on a 1,520 px 24-hour timeline ≈ 0.35 px; in b3 each token's coral block is drawn at the load block's original 180 px, because each token reads the same 140 GB the load moved
H100 41.8 ms, H200 29.2 ms (the 'thirty milliseconds'), B200 17.5 ms per token
bars at 20 px per ms: 836 / 583 / 350 px; 30 ms marker at 600 px (x 1140 from the x 540 baseline)

s05 layout: from the x 540 baseline the bars end at x 1376 / 1123 / 890 and the 30 ms line is at x 1140, so the H200 bar stops 17 px short of the line: its '29.2 ms' goes past the line (x 1160) and the '≈ 30 ms' stamp sits above the line's top, not on the row
s05.b3 what-if: a 70 GB model halves every bar to 418 / 292 / 175 px (20.9 / 14.6 / 8.75 ms)
tokens per second = 1 ÷ time per token: H100 23.9 ('about twenty-four', the later fig 130 figure), H200 34.3, B200 57.1
the rounded 30 ms gives 33.3 tokens/s, against 34.3 from the exact 29.2 ms; shown on screen ('rounded from 30 ms') rather than hidden
